modern: You do not have the leisure or the ability to read. But you have the leisure, or the ability, to check arrogance: you have the leisure to rise above pleasure and pain: you have the leisure to rise above the love of fame, and not to be irritated at stupid and ungrateful people—indeed, even to care for them.
original: Thou hast not leisure [or ability] to read. But thou hast leisure [or ability] to check arrogance: thou hast leisure to be superior to pleasure and pain: thou hast leisure to be superior to love of fame, and not to be vexed at stupid and ungrateful people, nay even to care for them.

explained.summary: You may not have time to read and study, Marcus tells himself, but that matters less than it seems. You always have time to check your arrogance, to rise above pleasure and pain, to stop chasing fame, and to keep from getting annoyed with foolish and ungrateful people, and even to care for them.
explained.today: Too busy for the book club or the course you meant to take? You still have room, in the queue or on the school run, to be patient with the person in front of you and not to care who noticed your work.
